title: What is the Role of Education?
author: Brooks, Barrett
summary: Guest post by Barrett Brooks, introduced by Dave Stuart Jr., asking what education is actually for before anyone commits to systems like the Common Core or universal college. Brooks surveys the shifting foci of education across history (trade, religion, STEM, liberal arts, basic literacy, professional training) and argues that no single focus is obviously right. He proposes instead to design from principles that build capable, self-directed humans: literacy, research, exposure, leadership, design thinking and sustainability. His thesis is that education should show people their own capacity and give them the courage to lead, and that no test can measure that. Brooks is explicit that he is a lay person, so the piece is a reflective provocation rather than an evidence-based argument.
points: Brooks catalogs six historical foci of education to show how contingent any given system's aims are.
He asks that the question education for what? be settled before commitments to systems such as the Common Core.
His six principles favor adaptable, self-directed learning skills over subject coverage, especially research as access and interpretation rather than memorization.
Leadership is treated as an educational outcome: every child should be given real responsibility and taught to define personal values and communicate them.
He closes by contrasting a principle-centered system with a test-centered one, arguing that no test gauges a person's ability to be a good human.
quotes: Would we not be better served to start with why we want to educate humans and then build a curriculum to suit that need?
What if we designed our education systems to build better humans by focusing on an adaptable set of skills? The kind of skills that lead to self-directed learning over the course of a lifetime.

Research – in a world where every book in history will one day be cataloged by Google; where any fact can be found in seconds; where any calculation can be performed automatically… the key skill will not be memorizing information, but accessing it. Organizing it. Interpreting it.

Children (and adults for that matter) don't need to be forced to learn topics, they simply need to be exposed to enough topics to find one they can get lost in. And if they don't learn the history of the industrial revolution, oh well!
It means that every child should be named captain of at least one team — not given a trophy, but given responsibility and encouragement to lead. Every child should be taught to make their own rules.
The best we can hope, and perhaps all we could ever hope from a great education: Show people their own capacity, and give them the confidence and courage to lead.
There is no test that will gauge a person's ability to be a good human and protect the world for future generations. Why do we pretend that there is?
